Response: We cannot agree with the reviewer’s conclusion so far. Based on the illustration in above replies, we believe one can find that our study has provided substantial and solid evidence supporting both the innovative nature of the catalyst and its potential for practical application.
Firstly, the transesterification route for 1,2-BC production is industrially competitive because it has cheap feedstock supply (especially based on coal industry) and solvent- free reaction conditions.
Secondly, regarding the mechanism, we have demonstrated the remote catalysis through a combination of in situ DRIFTS, XAFS, XPS, DFT calculations, wherein the adsorption investigation has provided straightforward evidence. These results consistently show that the isolated Bi atoms modulate the electronic structure of adjacent Ce sites and O sites, thereby enhancing the reactant adsorption, reducing the energy barrier of the rate- determining step, and enabling a unique exothermic desorption process, without direct contact with the reactant or product.
Besides, we have conducted experiments with over ten diol substrates (Supplementary Table 18) and a long-term stability test up to 1400 h, far longer than that in most literature. These results robustly confirm the broad applicability and exceptional durability of the Bi - 1 CeO catalyst, showing good potential for industrial application.
This manuscript reports an unprecedentedly highly active (2499 g g -¹ h-¹) and long- 1,2-BC cat. lived (800 h) Bi -ceria catalyst, which exhibits significant advantages in ester exchange 1 reactions, far exceeding the catalyst performance reported in existing literature. The "remote catalysis" mechanism was proposed, that is, the Bi1 single atom enhances the reaction performance by regulating the adjacent Ce³⁺-O acid-base site (rather than directly serving as the active center), providing a new idea for the design of single-atom catalysts (SACs). It was found that the Bi1 site dynamically reconstructs into BiOx and can be regenerated through simple heat treatment, providing important insights into the deactivation and regeneration mechanism of the catalyst. It is recommended to carry out a major overhaul.

We are confident that the above justifications and the potential refinements will be able to effectively convey the significance of this study, academic novelty, and practical implications, and sincerely hope to have the opportunity to submit an updated manuscript for reconsideration.

Q1. Mechanistic clarification and remote catalysis validation
The authors have expanded their mechanistic discussion of the “remote catalysis” concept, integrating evidence from XPS, CO /NH -TPD, in situ DRIFTS, and DFT calculations. 2 3 These results support the idea that Bi single atoms electronically modulate adjacent Ce sites rather than directly participating in the reaction. However, as acknowledged by the authors, the quantitative range of the electronic propagation and its spatial extent remain speculative. Please supplement further studies on how variations in Bi doping concentration influence the structure and catalytic behavior would greatly strengthen this novel concept.
R1: We thank the reviewer for their positive comment on the proposed concept of “remote catalysis”. Following the suggestion by the reviewer, we have carried out additional experiments with various Bi doping concentrations and investigated their influence on catalytic performance and the catalyst structure.
• Catalytic performance
We carried out additional catalytic performance of 0.2% Bi-CeO -R, 1.0 % Bi-CeO -R and 2 2 5.0 % Bi-CeO -R (Fig. R1 & updated in Fig. 1F). When using pure CeO as catalyst, the 2 2 conversion of 1,2-BDO was only 26.5%. After doping 0.2% Bi on CeO , the conversion 2 increased to 57.4%. By increasing the Bi content to 0.6%, the optimal conversion of 87.4% was achieved. However, when the Bi content continued to increase, the conversion of 1,2- BDO eventually dropped to 24.7% with 5% Bi, indicating a proper content of Bi doping is essential for the best catalytic behavior, this is because such transesterification reaction needs moderate acidity and strong basicity, which has been evidenced by the XPS and TPD tests and detailed discussed in the manuscript (lines 181-221). These results confirm that the reaction is promoted by Bi in an indirect manner of “remote catalysis”, which altering the acid-basic sites in an appropriate extent.

• Catalyst structure
The actual content in the synthesized catalysts are summarized in Table 1 (updated in SI Supplementary Table 2 and lines 342-343), which were determined by inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES). The X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of both the pristine CeO and the x%Bi-CeO series catalysts (Figure R2 & 2 2 updated in Fig. 1C and lines 119-125) mainly show the diffraction peaks of CeO (JCPDS- 2 34-0394), and peaks for Bi species were not detected, indicating the high dispersion of Bi on the CeO surface. However, we found that with the increase of Bi content up to 1%, the 2 CeO (111) diffraction peak shifted toward lower angles, suggesting the lattice expansion 2 of CeO with the incorporation of Bi species. When Bi content is excessively high to 5%, 2 partial oxide species were formed (Supplementary Figures 48-53), and the lattice expansion effect is weakened.

Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy was employed to further elucidate the structural influence of Bi species doping on the CeO lattice (Figure R3 & 2 updated in Fig. 2E and lines 173-180). 0.2%Bi-CeO catalyst aroused stronger spin signal 2 compared to pristine CeO , which is consistent with the conclusion in the manuscript in 2 lines 171-172, “More importantly, the volcano relationship reveals that the addition of Bi may enrich O 1, which would then affect the catalytic activity2.” This indicates that the v incorporation of Bi species can promote the concentration of O . 0.6%Bi-CeO saw a v 2 notable enhancement in the EPR signal, suggesting the highest concentration of O . As v noted in the manuscript, “Bi -CeO shows a stronger spin signal at g = 2.003 (Fig. 2E), 1 2 about seven times that of pristine CeO (Supplementary Table 6), indicating more O with 2 v Bi present.” The generation of a high density of O promotes a substantial increase in Ce3⁺ 1 v content, resulting in a decrease of positive charge on Ce atoms near O and an increase v in the negative charge on the adjacent oxygen atoms. This electronic modification leads to enhanced basicity and provides abundant moderate acid active sites on the catalyst, which further evidenced by the CO /NH -TPD profiles and Bader charge analysis in manuscript 2 3 Figure 2F and Figure 2I. As elaborated in the manuscript, “Bader charge analysis shows that the presence of O leads to less charge on Ce adjacent to the defects (+2.27 e), v compared to intact CeO -nonO (+2.32 e), and this change is further enhanced by the 2 v presence of Bi (Bi -CeO -O , +2.23 e), in line with the weaker acidity observed in 1 1 2 v experiments (Supplementary Fig. 15). Moreover, O atoms adjacent to O carried negative v charge of -1.15 e and -1.21 e for CeO -nonO and CeO -O , respectively. In the presence 2 v 2 v of Bi , the negative charge on the O atom is increased to -1.23 e, in line with the strong 1 basicity observed in experiments.” However, it should be noted that when the Bi content increases to 5% (as shown by the EXAFS results in Supplementary Figures 48-53), the presence of excessive oxide (not detected by XRD, Figure R2) may cause a significant decrease in the effective O concentration on CeO surface, leading to a corresponding v 2 reduction in catalytic activity (Figure R1)3.

The microscopic structure of the catalyst and acid-base properties are found sensitive to the Bi content. To get more insights on this perspective, we supplemented an additional in situ DRIFTS study using the catalysts with more Bi loadings. As demonstrated in our manuscript (Figure 3) and Supplementary Information DFT calculations (Supplementary Figures 16-33, Tables 9-10), our combined in situ DRIFTS and DFT analysis has established that Ce sites adjacent to O serve as the primary active sites for 1,2-BDO v adsorption. The bridged butoxy-O conformation has been identified as the active v adsorption conformation, whereas the top-butoxy and bridged-butoxy conformations are catalytically inert, as stated in the manuscript: "In contrast, only on-top butoxy adsorption conformation (1086 cm-1) was observed on the Bi O surface that is proven to be inactive 2 3 for transesterification (Supplementary Fig. 17). The adsorption behavior of 1,2-BDO on Bi - 1 CeO -C and Bi -CeO -O was also compared, and on-top butoxy (~1100 /1098 cm-1) and 2 1 2 bridged butoxy (~1069 /1071cm-1) have been identified on both samples, which are inactive neither for the transesterification reaction (Supplementary Fig. 18-19)".
As shown in Fig. R4, the supplemented in situ DRIFTS spectra collected at room temperature revealed three distinct butoxy conformations on the highly active 0.6%Bi- CeO catalyst: top-butoxy (1091 cm-1), bridged-butoxy (1062 cm-1), and the key bridged- 2 butoxy-O conformations (1035 cm-1) (Figure R4B). With the temperature increase to 403 v K, the inert top-butoxy and bridged-butoxy conformations were progressively transformed to the bridged-butoxy-O conformation (Figure R4E). In contrast, the 0.2%Bi-CeO catalyst v 2 exhibited a tri-coordinated-butoxy conformation (1018 cm-1) at room temperature (Figure R4A). Even at 403 K, the peaks of inert top-butoxy (1091 cm-1) and tri-coordinated (1033 cm-1) species persist, rationalizing its lower activity (Figure R4D). For the excessively doped 5.0%Bi-CeO , the room-temperature spectrum was dominated by top-butoxy (1098 2 cm-1) and bridged-butoxy-O (1039 cm-1) conformations. The elevated temperature up to v 403 K not only saw the intensified top-butoxy signal but also led to the transformation of the bridged-butoxy-O species (1039 cm-1) into inactive bridged-butoxy (1051 cm-1) and tri- v coordinated-butoxy (1030 cm-1) conformations, explaining its poor performance at the reaction temperature (Figure R1). These results demonstrate that varying the Bi content dominants the 1,2-BDO adsorption conformation, in well agreement with our DFT calculation results and that the optimal doping of 0.6%Bi is most favorable for the formation of cyclic carbonates.

Regarding the DMC adsorption, a comparative analysis of DMC adsorption was carried out on catalysts including the inactive Bi -CeO -O and Bi O , and the highly active Bi - 1 2 2 3 1 CeO -R, Bi -CeO -C, and CeO . The results revealed that the cis-cis monodentate 2 1 2 2 adsorption conformation based on the C=O-Ce-O motif is the primary active species v (Supplementary Figures 23–29; lines 267–275). DFT calculations further confirm that Bi species directly influence the adsorption behavior of DMC (in manuscript lines 275–278), as noted: “This is consistent with the DFT results, where the cis-cis-monodentate C=O-Ce- O binding has the highest adsorption energy of -1.04 eV (Supplementary Table 9 & v Supplementary Fig. 32). The calculations show that O facilitates 1,2-BDO adsorption (1,2- v BDO-4 and 1,2-BDO-5), while Bi impacts on the DMC adsorption (DMC-2 and DMC-6, 1 Supplementary Fig. 32-33 & Supplementary Table 9-10)”.
We implemented additional in situ DRIFTS test as shown in Figure R5, to illustrate the influence of Bi content to DMC adsorption behavior. Over 0.2%Bi-CeO , the intensity of 2 the cis-cis monodentate conformation (1766 cm-1) at room temperature is slightly stronger than that of the inactive bidentate conformation (1780 cm-1), as shown in Figure R5. When the temperature rose to 403 K, the adsorption band shifted to 1772 cm-1 (Figure R5D). In contrast, the cis-cis monodentate conformation (1766 cm-1) is distinctly dominant on the 0.6%Bi-CeO surface (Figure R5B). At 403 K, the cis-trans monodentate conformation 2 (1750 cm-1) transforms to cis-cis monodentate conformation, and the cis-cis monodentate conformation remains predominant. Over 5.0%Bi-CeO , a significant amount of the cis- 2 trans monodentate conformation (1745 cm-1) was present. Upon 403 K, the inactive bidentate conformation (1779 cm-1) becomes the dominant species. These observations clearly explain the changes in catalytic activity presented in Figure R1. Together with the DFT modelling of reactants adsorption, the results verify that while Bi species do not serve as the direct active sites, they modulate the catalyst’s acidity/basicity, which in turn governs the adsorption conformation of DMC and ultimately dictates the catalytic performance.

In summary, in the “remote catalysis” context, Bi species serves to electronically engineer the active sites of Ce and O atoms on CeO catalyst remotely, thereby refining 2 the material's acid-base properties. This coordination change facilitates the preferential formation of the active cis-cis monodentate conformation for DMC and the bridged-butoxy- O conformation for 1,2-BDO. These specific conformations of DMC and 1,2-BDO v contribute to their simultaneous activation and the unprecedented catalytic performance.
We believe the above supplementary experiments and illustrations would well address the concern from the reviewer in terms of “remote catalysis”. All relevant sections of the manuscript and Supplementary Information have been updated accordingly to reflect this mechanistic insight.
